verifyNote: Written from standard UK contact lens practice (BCLA / College guidance). Always check against Dr Dutta's slides — fitting rules of thumb and grading conventions vary between lens designs and departments.

topics.title: Introduction, history and symptoms
topics.summary: CLB Lecture 1 (Dr Dutta, week 1): why people choose contact lenses, how contact lenses developed, what modern contact lens practice covers, and how to take a contact lens history and symptoms, spot contraindications and take the baseline measurements (HVID and pupil size).
keyPoints: Why contact lenses: more natural vision and a wider field (no frame), optics stay aligned with the eye, no fogging or rain on lenses, better for anisometropia and irregular astigmatism, good for sport and under goggles, cosmetic benefits, UV protection and myopia control.

Contact lens practice now covers optical correction, myopia control, therapeutic/medical lenses (after disease, surgery or trauma), aesthetic lenses and specialist uses (e.g. drug delivery, scleral lenses).

Lens types: spherical or toric, single vision or multifocal; rigid gas permeable (corneal or scleral); soft (hydrogel or silicone hydrogel); daily disposable, planned replacement or reusable; plus ortho-K. Silicone hydrogel wear is increasing.

History structure: patient preferences (why CLs, current lens/brand/modality, years of wear, hours per day, solution, quality-of-life benefits), lifestyle (age, recreation, occupation and hobbies, environment, digital devices), health (general and ocular health, surgery, medication, family history, allergies) and refractive state (spherical, astigmatic, presbyopic, paediatric/myopia).

Symptoms: use SOCRATES — site (one or both eyes), onset, character (glare, blur; burning, gritty, itchy, watery, tired), timing, exacerbating/relieving factors (near/distance, with lenses) and severity.
Medication matters: some systemic drugs reduce tear volume or blink rate, or change corneal sensitivity; topical drops and their preservatives can be absorbed by soft lenses.
Baseline measurements: HVID (range about 10–14 mm, average 11.7 mm), pupil size in room and dim light, and keratometry/topography.
examTraps: Forgetting to ask about medication — it can reduce blinking and tear volume and cause lens intolerance.
Measuring pupil size only in room light — dim-light size matters for presbyopic and myopia-control designs.
Skipping pre-fitting counselling (risks, costs and what to do in an emergency) and not documenting it.

diagram.description: Timeline of contact lens history: early ideas (Celsus, Da Vinci, Descartes 1637, de la Hire 1685), Thomas Young 1801, John Herschel 1827, then Fick, Kalt and Müller in the late 1880s, and Zeiss lathe-cut lenses.

goDeeper.heading: A short history of contact lenses
goDeeper.body: Early ideas don't really describe contact lenses: Celsus used linen discs after pterygium surgery; a Leonardo da Vinci manuscript was long thought to show the 'invention' of contact lenses (later disproved); Descartes described a water-filled tube (1637) and de la Hire a fluid that might correct myopia (1685). Thomas Young (1801) and Sir John Herschel (1827) deserve more credit — Herschel suggested that for badly irregular corneas a transparent jelly in a glass capsule, or a mould of the cornea, could give clear vision. In the 1880s Adolf Fick made moulded lenses (from rabbit and cadaver eyes) and tried them on himself, Eugène Kalt noticed lenses could change corneal shape, and August Müller, a −14.00 D medical student, corrected his own myopia with glass lenses he could wear for about 30 minutes. Zeiss later lathe-cut lenses, giving better optics and the first commercial trial lenses.

goDeeper.heading: Conditions and contraindications
goDeeper.body: Ask about allergy and hay fever (atopy), diabetes, systemic inflammatory disease such as sarcoidosis (uveitis), thyroid eye disease, skin conditions linked to blepharitis (seborrhoeic dermatitis, atopic eczema, acne rosacea) and previous eye surgery — with onset, type, how well controlled, and family history. Possible contraindications include a very low refractive error, a need for horizontal prism, eye infection or inflammation, recurrent corneal erosion, diabetes, sinus and allergy problems, sensitive or dry eyes and poor blinking, acne rosacea or seborrhoeic conditions, and adverse (e.g. dusty) environments. Considering these first saves everyone time and money.

goDeeper.heading: Medication and contact lens wear
goDeeper.body: Systemic: antihistamines, antidepressants and diuretics can reduce tear production; tranquillisers, muscle relaxants and alcohol can reduce blink rate and amplitude; oestrogens and some pain relievers can change corneal sensitivity; blood pressure drugs and anticholinergics can affect vision; some drugs affecting fluid balance can cause corneal oedema. Topical: soft lenses (especially hydrogels) can absorb and retain drops and their preservatives, which can cause irritation or toxicity. Review medications at every visit.

goDeeper.heading: Before fitting: counselling
goDeeper.body: Discuss and document: the recommended lens type, modality of wear, care and cleaning regimen, possible risks and complications, how long until full-time wear, possible visual compromise or discomfort, what to do in an emergency, and the costs involved.

goDeeper.heading: Baseline measurements
goDeeper.body: HVID (horizontal visible iris diameter) can be measured with a topographer, autorefractor, slit lamp graticule, aberrometer or PD ruler — normal range about 10–14 mm, average 11.7 mm. Measure pupil diameter with a ruler (or Burton lamp) in room light (photopic, average) and dim light (scotopic, maximum) — important for presbyopic and myopia-control lenses. Add K readings or topography, and corneal shape/scleral dimensions if needed. Vertical palpebral aperture is rarely used nowadays.

cases.scenario: A 51-year-old wants contact lenses for tennis. She has hay fever and takes antihistamines in summer, works long days on a laptop, and wears varifocals (add +1.50).
cases.question: What would you focus on in her history and before fitting?
cases.modelAnswer: Explore her reasons and wearing times (sport), atopy and antihistamine use (dryness, possible daily disposables in hay fever season), screen use and symptoms (SOCRATES), general and eye health. She's presbyopic, so discuss multifocal CLs or monovision and measure pupil size in room and dim light; take HVID and K readings. Counsel on lens type, wear, care, risks, costs and emergencies, and document it.

topics.title: Keratometry
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 3 lecture: the keratometer measures the radius of the central cornea (really the tear film acting as a convex mirror) in its two principal meridians. Know how it works, what it assumes, where errors come from and what you use it for.
keyPoints: The cornea gives about two thirds of the eye's power (about 43 D). Radii range from about 7.4 to 8.8 mm; record e.g. 7.90 @ 150; 7.85 @ 60.
Principle: an object of known size at a fixed distance is imaged by the cornea as a convex mirror; radius ≈ 2 × working distance × image height ÷ mire separation.

Working distance is checked with a Scheiner disc (doubled image unless aligned); eye movement is overcome by doubling the image with a prism. Fixed doubling (Bausch & Lomb, one position) or variable doubling (Javal-Schiotz, two positions).
Assumptions: a spherical arc, principal meridians at 90°, an on-axis measure, and a back surface with −10% of the front power, hence n = 1.3375 (USA: D = 0.3375 ÷ r).
Errors: operator (focusing, proximal accommodation, alignment, orientation) and patient (corneal distortion, unsteady fixation). Distorted mires suggest an irregular cornea.
Uses: baseline data, corneal astigmatism (0.05 mm difference ≈ 0.25 D), choosing a first lens and whether RGP or toric is needed, RGP flexure, post-wear oedema or moulding, and verifying lens radius.
In clinic: take three readings of each meridian in each eye and average them.
examTraps: Forgetting it only samples a small central area (about 3 mm): topography maps the rest.
Mixing up meridian and axis when recording.
Assuming refractive astigmatism equals corneal astigmatism: lenticular astigmatism can differ.

diagram.description: Two corneal topography maps side by side. Left: regular with-the-rule astigmatism — a symmetrical vertical 'bow tie' of warmer (steeper) colours. Right: keratoconus — an asymmetric patch of hot colours inferiorly. Colour scale bar: red/orange = steep, blue = flat.
labels: Colour scale: red = steep, blue = flat

goDeeper.heading: Test-your-knowledge answers
goDeeper.body: Keratometry readings represent corneal curvature, in millimetres or dioptres. A hyperbola has e² over 1. Against-the-rule astigmatism gives a horizontal bow tie on a topography map.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: HVID and pupil size
goDeeper.body: Horizontal visible iris diameter (about 11.5–12 mm) and pupil size are measured alongside K readings to choose total diameter and optic zone; the week 5 rigid lens lecture gives the rules (TD about 2 mm less than HVID; BOZD about 1 mm larger than the pupil).

flashcards.back: About 45.00 D.
Vertical meridian steeper than horizontal.
Asymmetric inferior steepening (hot colours inferiorly).
Bausch & Lomb: fixed doubling, both meridians measured from one position. Javal-Schiotz: variable doubling, two positions.
Focusing, proximal accommodation, alignment and orientation of the instrument.

The vertical meridian (90) has the smaller radius, so it's steeper — with-the-rule.
0.30 is the difference in mm, not dioptres.
Convert each radius to dioptres and subtract.

mcq.explanation: Convert each K to dioptres with 337.5/r and subtract. The steeper (smaller radius) meridian tells you the type.

mcq.q: Refractive astigmatism is −2.00 × 180; corneal astigmatism is 2.00 D with-the-rule. With a spherical RGP, what residual astigmatism would you expect?

That would be the case if it were all lenticular.
They don't add; the tear lens cancels corneal astigmatism.
Comparing refractive and corneal astigmatism lets you estimate it.

mcq.explanation: Residual astigmatism ≈ refractive astigmatism − corneal astigmatism (in matching form). Equal amounts at matching axes leave little residual.

topics.title: Soft lens materials: hydrogel and silicone hydrogel
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 9 and week 12 lectures: what an ideal soft lens material needs, how oxygen reaches the cornea and is measured (Dk, Dk/t, EOP), what hypoxia does, how wettability is tested, and how hydrogels and silicone hydrogels compare.
keyPoints: Ideal material: meets the cornea's oxygen needs, inert, wets well, resists spoilage, biocompatible and comfortable, dimensionally stable, durable, transparent, low-maintenance and easy to make.

Corneal oxygen comes from the air with eyes open, the palpebral conjunctiva with eyes closed, plus the limbus and aqueous. Air is 21% oxygen; under closed lids about 8%; the cornea swells 3–4% overnight anyway.
Dk (permeability) = diffusion × solubility, a material property quoted at 34°C (range 0–300 × 10⁻¹¹). Dk/t (transmissibility) depends on thickness (range 0–200 × 10⁻⁹).
The original Fatt method overestimates Dk (edge and boundary effects); corrected values are about 25% lower and coulometric values 5–10% lower again. EOP results depend heavily on method.
Holden-Mertz: Dk/t 24 (EOP 9.9%) for daily wear and 87 (EOP 17.9%) for extended wear; later estimates 35 and 125 (Harvitt and Bonanno) or 175 (Smith et al.).
Low Dk/t causes microcysts, oedema (striae), lower corneal pH, endothelial blebs and polymegethism, and neovascularisation.

Hydrogel Dk rises with water content but can't reach extended-wear needs. Silicone hydrogels separate oxygen (silicone) and water (hydrogel) pathways: first generation surface-treated, second internal wetting, third non-TRIS (e.g. comfilcon), then water-gradient designs.

Silicone hydrogels remove hypoxic complications; early generations had more mechanical events; mucin balls can occur; CIE and MK rates are unchanged when modality is matched. Hydrogels like etafilcon A still give a quiet eye in daily wear.
examTraps: Mixing up Dk (material) and Dk/t (lens).
Assuming more water means more oxygen in silicone hydrogels: that's only true for hydrogels.
Thinking silicone hydrogels lowered the rate of microbial keratitis: they didn't.

diagram.description: Graph with water content (%) on the x-axis and Dk on the y-axis. Hydrogel line rises gently with water content. Silicone hydrogel points sit much higher on the y-axis at lower water contents. Dashed horizontal lines mark daily-wear and overnight-wear oxygen thresholds (in Dk/t terms).
labels: Silicone hydrogel: high Dk, lower water

goDeeper.heading: Wettability tests
goDeeper.body: Sessile drop (water on the lens; under 90° is more wettable), Wilhelmy plate (advancing and receding angles as the lens is dipped) and captive bubble (air bubble under a lens in water, where advancing and receding angles are reversed). Poor wetting means worse vision, more deposits, discomfort and a home for microbes.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: thickness and modulus
goDeeper.body: Thicker lenses (high plus, toric ballast) have lower Dk/t, so check centre and peripheral thickness. Stiffer (higher modulus) silicone hydrogels can cause more mechanical problems such as SEALs and papillary conjunctivitis in some wearers.

flashcards.back: Dk = material permeability; Dk/t = transmissibility of a lens of thickness t.
About 24 × 10⁻⁹ Dk/t.
About 87 × 10⁻⁹ Dk/t.
Dk increases as water content increases.
Epithelial microcysts, stromal oedema (striae), endothelial blebs and polymegethism, neovascularisation.

flashcards.front: Oxygen at the cornea: open versus closed eye
flashcards.back: About 21% versus 8%.

options.feedback: Yes — Dk/t is inversely proportional to thickness.
Plus lenses get thicker centrally, lowering Dk/t.

mcq.explanation: Dk/t = Dk ÷ thickness, so for the same material a thinner lens transmits more oxygen.

mcq.q: A patient wants to sleep in lenses occasionally. Which material is more appropriate?

options.feedback: Right — overnight wear needs much higher oxygen transmissibility.
Hydrogels can't reach overnight oxygen requirements.

options.feedback: Overnight wear risk depends on oxygen and lens approval.
This gives the least oxygen of all.

mcq.explanation: Closed-eye wear needs high Dk/t (Holden–Mertz ~87 × 10⁻⁹), which in practice means silicone hydrogels licensed for it — and it still carries more infection risk.

mcq.q: What does Dk/t describe?

options.text: Oxygen transmissibility of a particular lens

options.text: Dk rises with temperature, and 34°C is near the corneal surface temperature

options.feedback: Yes: a flatter drop wets better.

topics.title: Soft lens fitting assessment
topics.summary: A good soft fit centres well with full corneal coverage, moves a little on blink, and passes the push-up test with moderate resistance. Assess after the lens has settled, and always check vision with an over-refraction.
keyPoints: Let the lens settle (about 5–20 minutes) before judging the fit.
Centration: full corneal coverage in all positions of gaze, with an overlap onto the conjunctiva all round.
Movement: a small amount on blink in primary gaze (roughly 0.2–0.4 mm) and some lag on upgaze/lateral gaze.
Push-up test: push the lens up with the lower lid; it should move with moderate resistance and recentre smoothly.
Tight fit: little or no movement, conjunctival indentation/blanching at the edge, vision may clear just after a blink.
Loose fit: lots of movement, decentration, edge lift, variable vision and discomfort.
Over-refract in the trial lens, then check VA and comfort.
examTraps: Judging the fit straight after insertion, before settling.
Calling a lens 'good' because it's comfortable — tight lenses often feel comfortable at first.
Using standard sodium fluorescein with soft lenses (it stains them).

diagram.description: Front view of an eye with a soft lens edge drawn as a circle beyond the limbus. Three versions: good fit (centred, even overlap), tight (centred but conjunctival vessels compressed at the edge, no movement), loose (decentred, edge visible on the cornea when looking up).

goDeeper.heading: The push-up test
goDeeper.body: With the patient looking straight ahead, use the lower lid margin to push the lens up gently. Grade the resistance: very loose lenses move with almost no force, very tight ones won't move. Many clinicians express it as a percentage tightness, aiming for around the middle (about 50%). Note how quickly the lens recentres when released.

goDeeper.heading: Fixing a poor fit
goDeeper.body: Too tight: try a flatter base curve or a smaller diameter (or a different material/design). Too loose: try a steeper base curve or a larger diameter. Change one thing at a time and re-assess after settling.

goDeeper.heading: Over-refraction and VA
goDeeper.body: Over-refract with spheres (and JCC for torics) over the trial lens. Vision that blurs and clears with blinking suggests a fitting problem rather than a power problem. If the lens is toric, check the orientation marks and use LARS ('left add, right subtract') to correct the axis for rotation.

checklist.title: Soft lens fit assessment
steps: Wash and dry hands; check the lens isn't inside out; insert.
Wait for the lens to settle (about 5–20 minutes).
Ask about comfort and vision.
Slit lamp, diffuse light, low magnification: assess centration and coverage.
Assess movement on blink in primary gaze.
Assess lag in up gaze and lateral gaze.
Do the push-up test and grade tightness.
Look at the edge for conjunctival indentation or edge lift.
Over-refract and record VA.
Record lens details and your fit assessment, and decide on the next step.

Moderate resistance (about 50% tightness) and smooth recentration.

options.feedback: You need to compensate for the rotation.
That's a 90° change; rotation compensation is the amount seen.

cases.scenario: A new soft lens wearer says the lenses felt great at the trial but by the end of the day her eyes are red and vision fluctuates. At aftercare the lens doesn't move on blink.
cases.question: What's going on and what do you do?
cases.modelAnswer: A tight fit: comfortable initially but causing limbal redness, reduced tear exchange and variable vision. Remove lenses, check the cornea and conjunctiva (staining, indentation), refit with a flatter base curve or smaller diameter (or different material), and review. Reinforce wearing time and hygiene advice.

topics.askClaude: Describe 4 soft lens fits to me in words (movement, centration, push-up, edges). I'll say tight, loose or good and what to change; correct me.

topics.title: Rigid lens design and fitting
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 4 and 5 lectures: why rigid lenses, their materials and naming, back-surface design, and the fitting routine from choosing a first trial lens to assessing dynamic and static (fluorescein) fit and adjusting power.
keyPoints: Benefits: sharper stable vision, good oxygen, durability, tailoring for irregular corneas and high astigmatism, deposit resistance, long-term cost. Good candidates: motivated, moderate to high Rx, stable toricity, residual cyl under 0.75 D.

Materials: PMMA (almost no oxygen, not a GP material), CAB, silicone acrylates, fluorosilicone acrylates (Dk 40 to 100+; Menicon Z, Dk 163, approved for 30 nights). USAN names: prefix, 'focon', formulation letter, group (I none, II silicone, III both, IV fluorine), Dk band.

Design aims: match the cornea, avoid indentation, keep tears exchanging, avoid lid irritation and decentration. Designs moved from constant axial edge lift to constant axial edge clearance (about 60–80 µm).
Tricurve: BOZD = TD − 1.4; secondary curve BOZR + 1.0 mm; peripheral curve BOZR + 2.5 mm. Ideal central tear layer 15–20 µm.
First BOZR from flat K and corneal astigmatism: under 0.50 DC, 0.05 mm steeper; 0.50–1.00 DC, 0.05–0.10 mm steeper; 1.00–2.00 DC, a third of the difference steeper; over 2.00 DC, toric.
TD about 2 mm smaller than HVID (usually 8.50–10.50 mm, ideally with upper lid attachment); BOZD about 1 mm larger than the pupil in average light. Plus and high powers are made larger.

Let the lens settle 10–20 minutes. Dynamic fit: comfort, coverage, centration and movement (grade 0 = 1.1–1.5 mm). Static fit: fluorescein with cobalt blue and a yellow filter, graded by zone in each meridian.
Sagittal depth decides fit: a steeper BOZR or bigger TD makes it steeper. Each 0.05 mm steeper BOZR adds +0.25 D of tear lens, so order 0.25 D more minus (and the reverse).
A spherical lens fitted on flat K on a with-the-rule cornea shows a horizontal band of alignment with pooling above and below.
examTraps: Calling a GP lens 'hard': hard means PMMA.
Changing BOZR without adjusting power for the tear lens.
Reading a with-the-rule band of touch as a flat fit.
Over-minusing the over-refraction: check with a +1.00 blur test. Ignore cylinders under 1.00 D.

diagram.description: Three circular RGP lenses on a cornea viewed under cobalt blue. Alignment: even pale green centrally with a bright green edge band. Steep: bright green central pool with a dark ring of touch mid-periphery and narrow edge band. Flat: dark centre (touch) with wide bright green edge stand-off.

goDeeper.heading: Worked power example
goDeeper.body: Trial lens 8.00 / −2.00, over-refraction −1.50: ordering 8.00 needs −3.50. Ordering 8.10 makes the tear lens 0.50 D more minus, so order −3.00.

goDeeper.heading: Aspheric rigid lenses
goDeeper.body: Pros: better capillary attraction, less flare, no transition pressure, thinner, easier to fit, less spectacle blur. Cons: corneal asphericity is hard to measure, centration can be poor, hard to verify and modify, and optics suffer if decentred.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: reading fluorescein patterns
goDeeper.body: Steep: central pooling (sometimes a bubble) with mid-peripheral touch. Flat: dark central touch, wide edge stand-off, decentration and rocking. Alignment: thin even central fluorescein, light mid-peripheral bearing and an edge band about 0.5 mm wide.

flashcards.back: Central pooling (bright green), mid-peripheral touch ring, narrow edge band.
Central touch (dark), wide edge stand-off, decentration/rocking.
Steeper add minus, flatter add plus.

flashcards.front: BOZR change per 0.25 D tear lens

topics.title: Care regimes, hygiene and patient instruction
topics.summary: Most serious contact lens problems come from how lenses are handled, cleaned and stored. Good teaching — insertion, removal, cleaning, case care and 'when to take lenses out' — is part of the fit, not an afterthought.
keyPoints: Wash hands with soap and dry them thoroughly before handling lenses.
Never expose lenses or cases to tap water, swimming pools, showers or hot tubs (Acanthamoeba risk).
Multipurpose solutions: rub and rinse (even if labelled 'no rub'), use fresh solution every time, never top up.
Hydrogen peroxide systems must be fully neutralised before wear (follow the recommended time).
Clean the case, leave it to air-dry face down, and replace it regularly (at least monthly or as advised).
Daily disposables avoid cases and solutions — a good option for many patients.
Don't sleep in lenses unless prescribed for it. If eyes aren't comfortable, seeing well and looking white, take lenses out and get advice.
examTraps: Saying 'no-rub' solutions don't need rubbing — rubbing removes more microbes and deposits.
Forgetting to mention water exposure when teaching care.
Not explaining what to do in an emergency (red, painful eye).

diagram.description: Soft lens balanced on a fingertip, viewed side-on. Correct orientation: a smooth bowl with edges pointing up. Inside out: the edges flare outwards like a saucer. Inset: 'taco test' — pinching the lens gently; edges curl inwards when correct.

goDeeper.heading: Teaching insertion and removal
goDeeper.body: Insertion: lens on the dry tip of the index finger, hold the upper lid by the lashes and pull the lower lid down, look up (or straight ahead) and place the lens on the eye, then look around and blink. Removal (soft): look up, slide the lens down onto the white of the eye with the index finger, pinch it off with thumb and finger. Do the right lens first every time to avoid mix-ups.

goDeeper.heading: Why water matters
goDeeper.body: Acanthamoeba lives in tap water and can bind to lenses and cases. Acanthamoeba keratitis is rare but very painful and hard to treat. That's why lenses, cases and solution bottles should never meet water, and lenses shouldn't be worn swimming (or should be daily disposables thrown away straight after, ideally with goggles).

goDeeper.heading: Compliance
goDeeper.body: Many wearers don't follow every instruction. Keep advice short and specific, demonstrate it, give written instructions, check understanding at each aftercare and ask open questions ('Talk me through what you do when you take your lenses out at night').

Explain cleaning (rub and rinse), fresh solution each time, no topping up.
Explain case care and replacement.
Explain no water exposure and no sleeping in lenses (unless prescribed).
Agree a wearing schedule and aftercare date.
Explain emergency advice: red, painful or blurry → lenses out, seek help.
Give written instructions and record what you taught.

topics.title: Aftercare and complications
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 10 lecture: about a third of wearers have some adverse event. Know the microbes involved, how lens wear affects defences, and how to recognise and manage microbial keratitis, the inflammatory and mechanical events, and contact lens dry eye.
keyPoints: Lens wear alters epithelial function (Dk/t dependent) and lowers PMNs and sIgA; most adverse responses follow bacterial colonisation of lenses. Daily wear increases lid and conjunctival bacteria, partly from the case.
Gram-positive (e.g. Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Corynebacterium) versus Gram-negative (e.g. Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Moraxella), which have an outer membrane.
Hypoxic changes: microcysts, vacuoles, bullae, oedema, neovascularisation, endothelial blebs and polymegethism.

Presumed MK: stromal infiltrate over 1 mm, more than mild pain, plus AC reaction, mucopurulent discharge or a positive culture. About 1–2 per 10,000 daily wearers a year; about 20 per 10,000 with overnight wear. Risks: hand hygiene, overnight wear, smoking, water, male sex.

MK management: hand hygiene, replacement and compliance, no overnight wear, early presentation; treatment with antimicrobials, cycloplegic, lubricants and later steroids. Daily disposables don't cut the absolute risk but cases are milder.

CLPU: single round peripheral infiltrate up to 2 mm with staining. CLARE: diffuse peripheral infiltration with small infiltrates, staining uncommon. IK: anterior stromal infiltrates with staining. CIEs: 0–0.4% a year in daily disposables, 2.5–7% with overnight reusables.
Mechanical: CLPC (papillae on the upper tarsus, more with non-ionic hydrogels, helped by frequent replacement), SEAL (grey-white superior arc), erosion (full-thickness epithelial loss).

Contact lens dry eye: CLIDE (symptoms only with lenses) or CLADE (pre-existing). Rule out other causes, then change care system, go daily disposable, change material or design, add lubricants, punctal plugs or omega-3, avoid harsh environments.
examTraps: Under-referring: pain plus an epithelial defect plus an infiltrate is presumed MK.
Confusing CLARE (no staining, after overnight wear) with MK.
Thinking daily disposables remove MK risk.

diagram.description: Three corneas side by side. MK: large central/paracentral grey-white infiltrate with stained epithelial defect, hypopyon in the AC. CLPU: small round peripheral infiltrate with a small stained defect. CLARE: scattered small peripheral infiltrates, red eye, no defect.

goDeeper.body: Avoid overnight wear; peroxide systems help. A young man with past CIEs or blepharitis, or someone with a high Rx, should be steered towards daily disposables.

goDeeper.body: Acanthamoeba keratitis causes pain out of proportion to the signs, a ring infiltrate and radial keratoneuritis, and is linked to water exposure. Treat any lens-related infiltrate with an epithelial defect as MK until proven otherwise.

topics.title: Grading scales (Efron / CCLRU) and recording
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 6 lecture: grading anterior eye findings lets you monitor change, tell normal from abnormal and hand over care. Use a named scale, grade to 0.1, and know the strengths of photographic and painted scales and of digital imaging.
keyPoints: Five-point scale: 0 normal (no action), 1 trace (action rarely needed), 2 mild (possibly), 3 moderate (usually), 4 severe (required). Add + or −, and extrapolate to conditions not on the card.

Grade to 0.1: a one-grade change is clinically significant, and rounding hides real change (2.5 to 3.4 both become 3). Inter-observer variation can reach 55%; 50 optometrists grading one image gave 1.2 ± 0.5.

Photographic scales (e.g. CCLRU) are realistic but need a huge library and vary in magnification, angle and patient. Painted scales (e.g. Efron) are less realistic but show severity systematically. Morphing sequences didn't improve grading.
Grade bulbar and limbal redness, palpebral redness and roughness, and staining (CCLRU staining by area: under 15% to over 45%). Always name the scale.
Digital imaging records what words can't and allows measurement. Consider the camera (CCD or CMOS; one-chip or three-chip), slit lamp optics, illumination, storage and support.

Resolution: the smallest features (microcysts, punctate staining, about 30 µm) need a 2 × 2 pixel matrix. Objective grading uses edge detection and colour extraction (red ratio for redness, green for staining), e.g. Keratograph 5M redness scans.
examTraps: Not stating which scale you used.
Grading only in whole numbers.
Thinking a painted scale is less useful than a photo: it shows severity steps more systematically.

topics.title: Corneal shape and topography
topics.summary: The cornea is aspheric: steepest at the apex and flattening towards the limbus. Keratometry samples a small central zone; videokeratoscopy maps 7 to 9 mm, and the kind of map you choose changes what you can read from it.
keyPoints: Corneal radii range from about 7.4 to 8.8 mm. A 0.05 mm difference between meridians is about 0.25 D of corneal astigmatism.
Asphericity: e² = 1 − p = −Q. Circle e² = 0; prolate ellipse 0 to 1 (the normal cornea, mean about 0.22); parabola 1; hyperbola above 1; oblate below 0.
Colour maps: warm colours are steeper (shorter radius), cool colours flatter.
With-the-rule astigmatism gives a vertical bow tie; against-the-rule gives a horizontal bow tie.

Axial (sagittal) maps: most repeatable, but distort the position of the apex. Tangential (instantaneous) maps: best for locating the apex and local changes. Height maps: the most direct shape measure, used for refractive surgery and simulated fluorescein patterns.
Topography shows things keratometry misses: irregular and asymmetric astigmatism, keratoconus, and orthokeratology treatment zones.
examTraps: Comparing two maps without checking the scale. Relative and absolute scales colour the same cornea differently.
Assuming topography measures the cornea directly. Placido systems read the tear film, so a poor tear film breaks up the rings.
Forgetting that a 2.5 mm decentration can create about 1 D of false astigmatism: alignment matters.

goDeeper.heading: Where videokeratoscopy goes wrong
goDeeper.body: Sources of error listed in the lecture: paraxial assumptions that are poor in the periphery, the image coming from the tear film, poor fixation, image quality, focusing, the same number of points being analysed per ring (area sampling bias), bowl size, number of rings, and alignment. Accuracy is best for the intermediate rings.

goDeeper.heading: Alignment
goDeeper.body: Ideally a map would be centred on the line of sight through the entrance pupil. The instrument instead lines up perpendicular to the cornea, towards its centre of curvature, so the map centre is often not the pupil centre.

topics.title: Tear film and contact lenses
topics.summary: A contact lens splits the tear film and depends on it for comfort, wetting and oxygen. Know where each layer comes from, what changes it, and how to measure tear quantity, quality and stability before and during lens wear.
keyPoints: Lipid: meibomian glands and glands of Zeis and Moll; 0.1–0.2 µm; reduces evaporation; seen as interference fringes.
Aqueous: main lacrimal gland (reflex) and accessory glands of Krause and Wolfring (basal); about 7 µm; carries ions, glucose, proteins (lysozyme, lactoferrin, lipocalin, IgA) and vitamin A.
Mucin: conjunctival goblet cells and corneal epithelium; makes the surface wettable and stops bacteria adhering.
Volume about 7 µl, made at about 1.2 µl/min, turned over every 5 minutes; open-eye osmolarity about 315 mOsm/kg.
Blink rate about 12/min, reduced by reading, hard tasks and screens; partial blinks cause 3 and 9 o'clock staining with rigid lenses.
Tests: quantity (Schirmer, phenol red thread, meniscus height), stability (TBUT, NIBUT), lipid (Tearscope), damage (fluorescein, rose bengal, lissamine green) and symptoms (OSDI).
examTraps: Calling TBUT a test of tear secretion: it measures stability. Schirmer and phenol red measure quantity.
Thinking fluorescein TBUT is non-invasive: the drop adds volume to the tear film. NIBUT avoids that.

goDeeper.heading: Proteins and lenses
goDeeper.body: Lysozyme is small and strongly positively charged, so it's drawn into negatively charged (ionic, methacrylic acid) hydrogel lenses. When proteins attach to a hydrophobic surface their 3D structure unfolds (denatures), which can trigger discomfort and inflammation.

cases.question: List the range of clinical dry eye tests and what each measures.
cases.modelAnswer: Quality and stability: NIBUT, TBUT and meniscus regularity [2]. Quantity: phenol red thread and Schirmer [2]. Lipid layer: Tearscope [2]. Surface damage: corneal and conjunctival staining [2]. Symptoms: OSDI questionnaire [2]. Bonus: osmolarity (TearLab) [1].

topics.title: Contact lens modalities, market and optics
topics.summary: How often lenses are replaced, why disposables became standard, why people stop wearing lenses, and the optical differences between contact lenses and spectacles.
keyPoints: Modalities: conventional (worn until worn out), planned or frequent replacement, and disposables (from 1987).

Disposables: fewer deposit problems (papillary conjunctivitis, red eyes, poor comfort and VA), fewer unscheduled visits, higher-water lenses possible, spares, simpler care, better management and more patient contact.
UK: about 4.75 million wearers, Europe's largest market. 20–50% of wearers drop out, half because of discomfort.
Wettability: sessile drop, Wilhelmy plate, captive bubble (in vitro); tear break-up (in vivo).
Measure contact lens BVP with a small focimeter stop; vertex distance correction Fcl = Fsp ÷ (1 − dFsp).
Myopes accommodate more in contact lenses than in spectacles (so may need a reading add sooner); hyperopes accommodate less.
Extended wear: up to 6 nights and 7 days; continuous wear: up to 30 nights. Any corneal compromise means daily wear only.
Daily versus extended wear decisions: corneal status, risk factors, Rx, tear film, lid integrity, environment, individual characteristics.
examTraps: Listing EOP as a wettability test: it measures oxygen at the cornea.

cases.question: Give the advantages of disposable contact lenses.
cases.modelAnswer: Half a mark each: fewer deposit-related problems (papillary conjunctivitis, red eyes, reduced comfort and VA); fewer unscheduled visits; higher-water lenses for better corneal physiology; spare lenses; simpler lens care; better patient management; more patient contact.

cases.question: What are the key considerations for daily versus extended wear?
cases.modelAnswer: Half a mark each: corneal status; risk factors; Rx; tear film; lid integrity; environmental factors; individual characteristics.
